reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Gastric volvulus is an abnormal rotation of the stomach, classified as organoaxial (around its long axis, more common and often associated with diaphragmatic defects) or mesenteroaxial (around the short axis)
The classic Borchardt triad of acute presentation is severe epigastric pain and distension, retching with an inability to vomit, and difficulty passing a nasogastric tube
It is frequently associated with a large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia, diaphragmatic defects, and lax gastric ligaments, and occurs across all ages including infants
Acute volvulus is a surgical emergency because rotation can obstruct and strangulate the stomach, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation
Chest and abdominal radiographs may show an abnormally positioned, distended gas-filled stomach, and CT confirms the rotation and any associated hernia

Initial management of acute presentation is resuscitation and attempted nasogastric decompression, followed by urgent surgery to reduce the volvulus, assess viability, and repair the predisposing defect
Chronic or intermittent volvulus causes recurrent postprandial pain, bloating, and early satiety and is easily overlooked
reference.pathophysiology: The stomach is normally anchored by the gastrohepatic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, and gastrophrenic ligaments and by its fixation at the oesophagogastric junction and pylorus. Laxity, elongation, or absence of these attachments, or a diaphragmatic defect such as a large paraoesophageal hernia, allows the stomach to rotate abnormally. Rotation of more than around 180 degrees produces a closed-loop obstruction at both the gastro-oesophageal junction and the pylorus. Progressive gaseous and fluid distension raises intragastric pressure and, together with twisting of the mesentery, compromises the blood supply. Unrelieved, this leads to venous congestion, ischaemia, full-thickness necrosis, and perforation with catastrophic sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic disease or malignancy
Large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia without volvulus
additionalInvestigations: Chest and erect abdominal radiographs showing an abnormally sited, distended stomach or intrathoracic gastric bubble
CT of the chest and abdomen to confirm rotation, define the axis, and identify a diaphragmatic defect
Contrast study demonstrating the site and level of obstruction where the patient is stable
Upper GI endoscopy in selected non-emergency cases (with caution)
Bloods including lactate and inflammatory markers to detect ischaemia
redFlags: Acute presentation with the Borchardt triad indicating a surgical emergency
Features of strangulation or ischaemia (severe unremitting pain, haemodynamic instability, rising lactate)
Inability to pass a nasogastric tube with progressive distension
Signs of gastric perforation with peritonitis and sepsis
reference.prognosis: Prompt reduction and repair of acute volvulus before ischaemia develops carries a good outcome, but delayed diagnosis with strangulation and necrosis is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Chronic volvulus generally does well after elective repair of the underlying defect, with low recurrence when fixation and hernia repair are adequate.
pitfalls: Mistaking acute volvulus for simple gastric dilatation and delaying surgery
Persisting with attempts to pass a nasogastric tube instead of recognising the emergency
Failing to assess gastric viability and repair the predisposing hernia or defect at operation
Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with a known large hiatus hernia and vague chronic symptoms
Underestimating the severity in elderly patients with atypical or referred pain
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Resuscitate and attempt nasogastric decompression as the immediate first steps in acute presentation
Undertake urgent surgery to detorse the volvulus, assess gastric viability and resect any necrotic stomach
Repair the predisposing defect at operation, most often a large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia, and secure the stomach with gastropexy
Consider endoscopic detorsion, with or without percutaneous gastrostomy fixation, in selected patients unfit for major surgery
Offer elective repair for chronic or intermittent volvulus to prevent strangulation
Monitor lactate and inflammatory markers to detect early ischaemia
Manage through emergency general surgery with anaesthetic and critical-care support
